suggestions.title: The Sting
suggestions.description: 1936, Depression-era Chicago: two grifters — Robert Redford's cocky young Johnny Hooker and Paul Newman's retired legend Henry Gondorff — assemble an entire fake betting parlour to take down a mob boss who ordered a friend's murder. The joy of it is the construction: nothing is what it looks like, every minor character is a plant, and the film teaches you the rules of the long con early so it can break them late. Marvin Hamlisch's ragtime score (built around Scott Joplin's 'The Entertainer') made a 70s hit out of 1902 piano music, and the production design is a gorgeously grubby sepia. Seven Oscars including Best Picture, Best Director and Best Original Screenplay — the last time a straight-up crowd-pleasing caper won the top prize, and still the best argument that a heist film can be built on charm rather than bodies. 8.3 on IMDb.

suggestions.title: Amadeus
suggestions.description: Vienna, 1780s, told through the bitter unreliable memory of court composer Antonio Salieri: the story of a competent, devout mediocrity who watches a vulgar, giggling, obscenely gifted boy write music he knows he could never conceive. Miloš Forman's film is not really a biography — it is a film about professional envy, divine unfairness and the terror of recognising true genius in your own rival, which is why it plays as sharply to anyone who has ever had a talented colleague as it does to classical music fans. F. Murray Abraham's Salieri and Tom Hulce's cackling Mozart are both extraordinary, the Prague locations double convincingly for Vienna, and the finale — Salieri transcribing the Requiem dictation — is one of cinema's great depictions of creative process. Eight Oscars including Best Picture, Best Director and Best Actor. 8.4 on IMDb.

suggestions.title: Cinema Paradiso
suggestions.description: A famous Italian film director gets the news that Alfredo, the projectionist who raised him in a Sicilian village after the war, has died — and the memories come back: the parish cinema, the censored kisses snipped out by the priest, the town watching its own dreams flicker on a wall. Giuseppe Tornatore's film is an unabashed love letter to movie-going as a collective act, and it earns the sentimentality because it is honest about the trade: the boy who leaves the village for a real life can never come back to it. Ennio Morricone's love theme is one of the most recognisable in film, and the final montage of spliced-together cut kisses lands like a punch. Best Foreign Language Film Oscar, Palme d'Or at Cannes, and the highest-rated film still unwatched on your own database. 8.5 on IMDb — the version to watch is the 155-minute original cut, not the shortened one.
